en: While the princely gray wolf lived,
Whenever roused, we went to war
And tested our strength.
The mountain ibex of Daңduu-Bash,
The cliff goat with its thick hide,
We would put into the tanning vat.
Before my fortunate mother,
Standing sole to sole and pulling,
We tore them apart piece by piece;
Our muscles were each as large as a fist—
Such was our former strength.
We held feasts and revelries,
Drinking kumis and courting girls,
Playing orompoi and winning prizes;
Such boundless games we played.
In the safe days of happiness,
While the joyous gray wolf lived,
When the multitude camped in delight,
Their cares forgotten,
With pleasure by day and games by night,
In those flourishing times,
When we had drunk our fill of kumis,
Red-dressed and slender-waisted,
The most graceful beauties—
When yesterday the girls and young wives watched us,
If bored, we went hunting roe deer;
Through ninety mattocks in a row
We shot our arrows,
And plunged into such delights.
When your vigor is still sound,
Then enter battle;
If your strength is whole,
Then fall upon the enemy,
And learn the measure of your prowess.
Take only what your power permits,
And exert your warrior’s strength.
Now put your vigor and might
Fully to the test.
Show courage and test your strength;
Test every bit of your former might.
Then Külchoro said:
“While the hero still lived,
When all my strength was at its height,
When I scorched sand and set stone aflame,
In the days when I raged,
Destroying lives and spilling blood,
In the days when I thirsted for battle,
When I grasped my sword and took up my spear,
And laid the enemy low,
Subduing all who faced me
And driving them before me,
When I sharpened
My red, Zulfiqar-like sword,
And crushed the hostile foe,
Chewing them to pieces,
When I spread tumult wherever I went
And threw all who resisted into panic,
When I wore armor
No flame could pierce to my flesh,
When I subdued the foes who shot at me
And drove them round—
Your uncle was strong as a lion;
Your poor uncle Choro
Had every power needed for combat.
While my lionhearted uncle lived,
We brandished battle-axes
And stood testing our strength;
When would we ever strike from afar?
Taking matchlock and bow in hand,
We tested our strength side by side,
And singled out our foes without relent.
While my panther uncle lived,
We were guardians of the people;
We bore the aspect of princes,
We were the black eyes of the spring,
We were panther-hearted heroes ourselves.
While the precious gray wolf lived,
We were red-flaming caps of steel,
A blazing crimson fire
That stirred strife wherever war cries rang.
While the panther lived,
We were dark, keen caps of steel,
The splendor of the foe when put to flight,
A darkly burning fire
No sudden assault could extinguish.
While my great warrior lived,
We were the wind in the narrow mountain pass.
Yielding to none who fought us,
We were champions, ravenous lions;
We were the gray wolf’s true eyes,
The very flower of heroes.
He broke through dead ends and opened roads,
And attacked whatever foe he met.
Konurbai came from the Khakan’s realm
To the lands along Ala-Too,
But while my warrior still lived,
He could not defeat him in combat.
Khans and Manchu lords were crushed;
When the seer in Beijing beheld my bearing,
He wept, saying, “He is no mere mortal.”
Thus the diviner in Beijing wept.
The great Kaldai rode out to war,
And Konurbai too was crushed;
Unable to endure my warrior,
The people of the Khakan wept.
When they diverted the flowing water
And left the Muslim people thirsty,
When the black Manchu and the countless Shibe
Were pressed hard by their Kaldai,
I crossed straight over and opened a road.
While my ruined uncle lived,
He never failed to raise laughter,
Yet burned to enter battle
And put his power and strength to the test.
My lion uncle was a champion;
Another mortal like my uncle
Will never again be fashioned
And given life in this world.
My towering uncle was a mighty hero—
Alas, this treacherous world!
No such warrior will arise from humankind.
His fortune was perfectly balanced;
If you could see inside that hero,
His heart was broader than the face of the earth.
A gray tiger upheld him;
No other soul could move as he did.
A dragon followed him,
A panther went beside him;
No mortal could defeat him when he advanced,
And no enemy dared confront him.
No man dared exchange blows with him;
When he fought in earnest, none survived.
Those who faced him fled the land,
And none who met him escaped alive.
When he charged in wrath
And grappled, he set men’s souls aflame.
When that dread-inspiring prince
Turned his front upon the foe,
He bore the form of a dragon;
When the hero turned his back,
He bore the majesty of six thousand warriors.
Ah, while the gray wolf lived,
We drew our bows and tested our strength,
Testing all our might.
Firing matchlocks and drawing bows,
Shattering every target,
We stood thundering in earnest
And slaughtered all who challenged us.
We heaped humiliation on those who would not yield;
Whenever an enemy closed with us,
I have been waiting for you.
I listened carefully to your words,
Calling you the legacy left by the noble one,
I made you my hope.
I gladly listened to your words,
Calling you the legacy left by the fierce warrior,
I made you my protector.
I watched you closely,
Thinking to bind the sole heir of the mighty lion
As a support around my waist,
And set out to avenge
My valiant gray-maned uncle,
To trample upon the head
Of Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
To scatter all his livestock,
And dig a well in his place of honor,
To unleash a great fusillade,
To hurl him down and, from his blood,
Drink by the double handful,
And gouge out both eyes
Of Kanchoro, the foe I never forget;
Though once we shared the same ancestry,
I would feast upon his flesh.
I would drain his blood by the spoonful
And end the anguish in my heart;
To unleash a terrible conflict—
Waking or sleeping, my desire
Is to avenge my gray-maned uncle.
Though countless herds fill the plains,
Whenever my falcon-like uncle Semetey
Comes suddenly to mind,
I flare and burn like fire,
And my life cannot be contained in my grasp.
When the towering gray-maned hero lived,
I was a glowing crimson ember;
There was none like me in the world,
I was a bullet ready to be fired,
Subduing the whole wide world,
A daredevil surpassing all mankind.
Without my hero, I became like snow;
I slaughtered those before me and laid them low,
I made the Manchus cry out,
And crushed the strongest
Of the coat-clad Chinese.
The khan upon the throne was slain,
All the finest of them were slain.
I asked the hero for his renowned swift gray horse
And mounted it,
Subduing all who faced me,
And drove them into Beijing.
Hear of your father, the hero who passed away;
Listen, my child Seytek:
By following him, I became a hero
And stood equal with heroes’ sons.
Orphaned, I came of age;
With difficulty I rejoined my people.
Left tiny as a louse, I grew mighty,
And among all creation became Choro the Great.
Such is my story, if you will hear it:
My wings were broken,
And I lost my fierce warrior,
The panther huge as a black mountain.
My lungs are rising into my mouth;
I stand here unable even to cough.
Bullets pierced and bound my chest—
Twelve charges and eighty bullets—
And I can no longer bear them.
I have no strength left to gird my waist,
No sheltered place in which to lie,
No mountain looming as my refuge,
No mighty warrior uncle
To sit as my protector.
I lack my two hands, dear as life,
Which shattered rocks in service.
Your uncle grieved in servitude,
For the fierce warrior who had sheltered him
Was lost to him.
I burned with grief at that loss,
But, my child, bold Seytek,
I knew the noble one had left an heir—
From the renowned, magnanimous gray-maned hero,
My Morning Star left to me as a gift,
The support for which I yearned,
The prop bound about my waist.
From the noble one gone to the next world,
My precious little one left behind.
In the marshes of Kara-Kyya,
When the massed enemy fired their guns
And surrounded the magnanimous hero,
My uncle had told me:
“If the orphan survives,
Make him your support.
Make the wooded Keng-Kol and broad Talas
His shelter,” he had said.
“Take the boy Seytek who remains
And make him your own child.”
When my uncle spoke and departed,
I blazed and burned with grief.
For the uncle who had gone before,
For brave Seytek left as his legacy—
I burned with longing for you.
Yesterday, when the panther vanished,
I wailed and lamented in grief,
Hoping my refuge Seytek would come.
My river valley and spring,
My champion beheld when death was near,
